did_you_know.text: The word “yidvenu” is connected with free will: the offering was given out of generosity, not by force.
In the Bible, the word “nechoshet” can refer to copper or bronze, so translations sometimes differ.
Tekhelet was an expensive blue dye; according to a common identification, such dye was made in antiquity from sea snails.
Shittim wood is usually identified with acacia wood, which suits the desert climate of the Sinai region.
The verse mentions lamp oil, anointing oil, and incense—materials intended for three different uses in the Tabernacle.
The onyx stones and the set stones were part of the High Priest’s garments, not merely decorations in the Tabernacle.
The Tabernacle was a portable sanctuary, fitting a people who wandered in the desert and had no permanent city yet.
The cubit was an ancient length unit based roughly on the distance from the elbow to the fingertips, but its exact length is uncertain.
The command never to remove the ark’s poles shows that the ark was designed for carrying, while the poles remained a permanent part of it.
The cherubim in the Bible are not described as winged babies; they are heavenly figures associated with protection and divine presence.
The cherubim face one another while also turning toward the cover, suggesting both mutual connection and attention to the sacred center.
The showbread consisted of twelve loaves, corresponding to the tribes of Israel, and was replaced every Sabbath.
A talent of gold was a very large unit of weight; common estimates place it at roughly thirty to thirty-five kilograms.
